name: Daniel Deal
occupation_background: 34-year-old who grew up in Courtice, Ontario and works as an information systems analyst in the carbon capture industry; previous jobs include labourer, rebar rodman, crane operator apprentice, facility manager and environmental remediation operator, including time on Fort McMurray oil sands projects. The Squamish Chief reports he has a construction management degree. He says he chose to move to Squamish and at one point lived out of a small car between rentals; his site does not say what year he arrived.
top_priorities: A Better Deal on Housing: wider range of housing, faster approvals, workforce housing
A Better Deal for Taxpayers: value for every dollar and a 1-year moratorium on property tax increases
A Better Deal on Infrastructure: roads, utilities and facilities that keep pace with growth, including Brennan Park
A Better Deal for YOU: regular town halls, reformed committees, better communication
Build the downtown parkade studied in 2020; free parking permits for locals, paid parking for visitors

supports.text: A one-year moratorium (pause) on property tax increases in his first year as mayor
District-owned, communal-style workforce housing so people who work in Squamish can get a foothold
Speeding up municipal approvals to reduce delays that drive up housing costs
A wider range of housing: rentals, townhomes, apartments and starter homes
Building the downtown parkade studied in 2020, funded by paid parking for visitors while locals park free with a permit
Giving Brennan Park Recreation Centre more attention (he cites a splash pad as a better use of money than some bike lanes)
Regular community town halls, published municipal performance measures, and enforcing Community Benefit Agreements on major projects
Splitting ('unbundling') District construction contracts among multiple trades/companies rather than awarding one firm the whole job

Adapting the Whistler Housing Authority’s employee home-ownership model so people who work in Squamish can live here (his written answers to a resident’s questions on jobs and business, posted online, Sept 2026)

Bringing back or updating the District’s 2013–2016 Investment Incentive Program to attract and keep businesses (his written answers to a resident’s questions on jobs and business, posted online, Sept 2026)

Filling in existing neighbourhoods first; later, “strategically expanding” the growth boundary for business as well as housing, without harming outdoor recreation (his written answers to a resident’s questions on jobs and business, posted online, Sept 2026)

Partnering with large industry, including Woodfibre LNG, under “proper agreements” so both the company and the town benefit (his written answers to a resident’s questions on jobs and business, posted online, Sept 2026)

opposes.text: The proposed 10-year Woodfibre LNG financial agreement: says the amount is too low relative to WLNG revenue, it would tie the hands of future councils, and the vote is being rushed (he told the Squamish Chief the decision should be left to the incoming council)
Relying on property tax increases to balance the budget ('We cannot keep relying on raising the property tax to make up for our mistakes')
Spending on certain bike lanes (he questions the Depot Road bike lanes) ahead of amenities residents are asking for
Charging Squamish locals for parking ('No Squamish local should be penalized to travel around the town')
Council's past decision not to proceed with a downtown parkade after the 2020 study

Council decisions to “immediately block or postpone” that lead to “endless lawsuits” with major employers (his written answers to a resident’s questions on jobs and business, posted online, Sept 2026)

growth.position: Don’t slow approvals; fill in existing neighbourhoods first, expand the growth boundary later
growth.summary: Says Squamish is growing quickly and services are not keeping pace. In written answers posted online in September 2026 he said there is more room to build within existing neighbourhoods before expanding the growth boundary, but that the boundary will eventually have to grow — for business as well as housing — without harming outdoor recreation.
growth.quote: I believe we have more room to infill before looking to expand our growth boundary.

housing_affordability.position: Strongly for more public money and land for below-market homes, and a required share in big projects
housing_affordability.summary: Platform calls for a wider range of housing (rentals, townhomes, apartments, starter homes), faster municipal approvals, and workforce housing. He told the Squamish Chief he wants District-owned, communal-style workforce housing.
housing_affordability.quote: To have some kind of housing where people can work here and have a communal-style living might give people the footing to be able to find a position here.

homelessness.position: Against clearing camps with nowhere to go; points to supportive housing on Government Road; wants the Province to pay
homelessness.summary: Daniel had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Daniel’s own answers are below.

policing.position: Against funding more RCMP; strongly for mental-health crisis teams; a community task force to free up bylaw staff
policing.summary: Daniel had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Daniel’s own answers are below.

taxes_spending.position: Strongly for holding taxes to inflation; against the Woodfibre tax deal; referendums on big projects
taxes_spending.summary: Proposes a one-year moratorium on property tax increases, prioritizing essential services and infrastructure before discretionary spending, publishing performance measures, and more transparency on major projects. Asked where he would cut, he pointed to certain bike lanes. He also wants Brennan Park to get more attention and to unbundle construction contracts.
taxes_spending.quote: Hey, this is our budget. We have to stay within this. We cannot keep relying on raising the property tax to make up for our mistakes.

environment_lng.position: Against the 10-year Woodfibre tax deal; against pressing the plant through permits
environment_lng.summary: Urges council to vote no on the proposed 10-year WLNG agreement, arguing the payment is too small relative to the company's revenue, inflation will erode it, it limits future councils' ability to tax industry, and the vote is rushed before the election. He says he is not against the plant itself and wants to work with the company. No stated positions on climate action, the estuary or wildfire; he works in the carbon capture industry.
environment_lng.quote: Squamish should not sell our long term financial leverage for short term gains. ... A no today isn't a no forever.

transportation.position: Against spending local money on bike lanes ahead of recreation; in the middle on regional transit
transportation.summary: Wants to build the parkade studied in 2020, funded by visitor-paid parking, with a free online permit for residents. He questions spending on some bike lanes and says cycling is not practical for many residents much of the year. His platform also promises 'transportation solutions that reduce congestion' without specifics.
transportation.quote: It's not reasonable to ask someone who lives all the way out in Brackendale to ride their bike in the rain, to go to the farmer's market, to pick up a loaf of bread.

economy.position: Strongly for cutting red tape; protect industrial land; bring back business incentives
economy.summary: Wants to make it easier to do business and says he is meeting business groups to understand their problems. In written answers posted online in September 2026 he said he would adapt the Whistler Housing Authority’s employee home-ownership model, improve on the 2015 Employment Lands Strategy, and bring back or update the 2013–2016 Investment Incentive Program. Earlier proposals (Squamish Chief): unbundling District construction contracts so more local trades share the work, and enforcing Community Benefit Agreements on major projects.
economy.quote: I would also like to look at bringing back or updating the Investment Incentive Program they rolled out back in 2013-2016.

parking.position: Build more downtown parking; against paid parking — if it comes, locals park free
parking.summary: Says the biggest thing he would have done differently is build a downtown parkade after the 2020 study. He wants paid parking for visitors only, with a free online permit (a windshield barcode) for residents, and the revenue put toward the parkade. His platform says 'No Squamish local should be penalized to travel around the town.' He says the 2020 study estimated the parkade would pay for itself in six years; the study itself gives a range of 2 to 12 years.
parking.quote: I read the 2020 study on the parkade …They estimated … (they) would cover the cost in six years. So we would have already been seeing profit on this parking, if they had just said yes.

compass.rationale: Economic lean is modestly right: a property tax moratorium, essentials-before-discretionary spending, cutting bike-lane spending and faster development approvals. This is tempered by support for District-owned workforce housing, taxing major industry more heavily and enforcing Community Benefit Agreements. There is almost no evidence on social-axis issues (policing, harm reduction, homelessness policy, climate), so social is left at 0.

answer_notes.q11: Although this is not top on my priority list. This has been requested by several locals, and I would like to look into the viability of this before making a decision.
answer_notes.q12: We should not have to borrow to make these improvements, this is something we can try and solve through private-public cooperation, as well as more fiscal responsible choices.
answer_notes.q18: This is a mixed government issue. Although, it impacts the community directly, regional, and municipal funding is necessary to make notable change.
answer_notes.q31: No, the unhoused, are a vulnerable group. Clearing and removing encampments without the proper social structure, will just lead to another encampment elsewhere.
answer_notes.q34: Investing in a beautiful town where everyone feels welcome will never be a poor investment.
answer_notes.q14:

answer_notes.q15: There are parcels of land that would be beneficial to sell off. Whereas I believe most of the land the District should hold onto, and lease to developers if needed. Ideally it would be nice to see district-owned and managed housing (albeit this is more expensive).
answer_notes.q16: I know that most airbnb hosts are chosing to not rent out their rooms

name: Sean Easton
occupation_background: Co-Executive Director of Zero Ceiling, a Whistler-based non-profit working to end youth homelessness (he took on leadership in 2017), and co-founder of DWIFT Housing Society, a Squamish non-profit aiming to sell homes at cost. He arrived in Squamish in 2011 as a whitewater rafting guide, later trained as a youth worker, co-built the multi-generational 'Heart House' with family, and recently launched the engagement collective Residents United.
top_priorities: Affordable Living: housing locals can afford, modernized transport, freeze property taxes for 2027
Accessible Amenities: splash park, indoor playground, fitness centre; care and services close to home
Accountable Leadership: authentic engagement, transparency, industry paying its fair share
Now and for generations to come: balance growth with what the environment can sustain
Resident-centered governance: measure success by outcomes for residents, not completed processes

supports.text: Freezing property taxes for 2027
Creating housing that locals can afford throughout their lives, including below-market home ownership through non-profit models like DWIFT

Using public land for non-profit affordable housing: DWIFT submitted an expression of interest to buy part of the District's Pioneer Way land for permanently affordable housing rather than have it sold to a private developer (the Dec. 2 delegation urging council to reserve the land was made by Zero Ceiling co-executive director Lizi McLoughlin)

New accessible recreation: a splash park, indoor playground and fitness centre (in his WLNG op-ed he says the need he hears most often is a second sheet of ice, updated pool facilities and improved change rooms)
Committing Woodfibre LNG money to a community-selected legacy capital project
Environmental monitoring to hold industry accountable
'Resident-centered governance': authentic engagement and measuring success by whether residents' needs are met
Pushing provincial and federal governments for Squamish's 'fair share' of funding; supporting local businesses

opposes.text: The proposed 10-year Woodfibre LNG agreement as written: says it doesn't guarantee lasting community benefit and the pre-election timing prevents meaningful public participation
Judging housing policy by units approved rather than affordability outcomes: says the District added over 25% to its housing stock while prices and taxes kept climbing
District capital-project cost overruns: says the last two District-managed capital projects went more than $20 million over budget
The 12.8% 2026 property tax increase, which he says has not delivered matching amenities or infrastructure
Leveraging land and resources for 'short-term profit' rather than long-term shared benefit

growth.position: Growing too fast: slow approvals until infrastructure catches up; judge each project on what it delivers
growth.summary: Says growth has outpaced essential infrastructure and amenities and pledges to 'balance growth with what our environment can sustain.' He argues that adding supply alone has not made housing affordable. His non-profit DWIFT favours 'gentle densification' (low-rise apartments and townhomes).
growth.quote: Balance growth with what our environment can sustain, so future development serves both people and the planet
growth.source_url: https://www.squamishchief.com/local-news/a-new-squamish-non-profit-aims-to-make-homeownership-more-affordable-9480990 (for the DWIFT sentence), with the year labelled

housing_affordability.position: Strongly for more public money and land, and a bigger required share of below-market homes; resident-restricted ownership
housing_affordability.summary: Housing is his professional field. He co-founded DWIFT Housing Society to build homes and sell them at cost (reported in 2024 as 25-30% below market) to middle-income households, and DWIFT sought District land on Pioneer Way for that purpose. His platform promises 'housing that locals can afford throughout their lives.'
housing_affordability.quote: Towns across B.C.—and the world—are getting creative in solving the housing and affordability crises, and I believe Squamish can, and must, too.

homelessness.position: Build the Pioneer Way and Hearth and Home supportive housing; against clearing camps with nowhere to go
homelessness.summary: He leads Zero Ceiling, which provides supportive housing and employment to young adults facing homelessness in the Sea to Sky.
homelessness.quote: These are people who often fall through the cracks—but I've always found that, when we listen to what they really need, and then take action, they can thrive here just as much as anyone else.

policing.position: In the middle on more RCMP and bylaw officers; strongly for crisis teams; hold everyone to the law, with services
policing.summary: Sean had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Sean’s own answers are below.

taxes_spending.position: Freeze property taxes for 2027; against the Woodfibre tax deal as written; pay for Brennan Park through industry, not debt
taxes_spending.summary: Pledges to freeze property taxes for 2027 and 'spend your dollars transparently and thoughtfully.' He criticizes the 12.8% 2026 tax increase, questions whether $21M spent at Brennan Park met residents' most pressing needs, and says the last two District capital projects ran more than $20M over budget. He also wants new recreation amenities, ideally funded through a renegotiated WLNG deal; he has not said what he would cut to fund the freeze.
taxes_spending.quote: ...they don't feel heard, and they don't feel their tax dollars are being spent effectively to make Squamish a place where they can thrive.

environment_lng.position: Use every tool to protect health, air and water from Woodfibre LNG; climate a priority, but not at residents’ short-term cost
environment_lng.summary: In a Sept 14, 2026 op-ed he asked council to reject the proposed 10-year WLNG agreement, saying about $14M a year is not enough to leave a lasting asset, the money should be committed to a community-selected legacy project, and the pre-election timeline shuts out the public. He wants robust environmental monitoring of WLNG. He has not said he opposes the plant itself; no specific positions found on climate policy, the estuary or wildfire.
environment_lng.quote: Making such a consequential decision under duress and without meaningful public engagement is irresponsible.

transportation.position: For regional transit if senior governments pay their share; pause new bike-lane spending until residents are consulted
transportation.summary: His platform promises to 'invest in modernized transport that meets our diverse needs' but gives no detail.
transportation.quote: Invest in modernized transport that meets our diverse needs

economy.position: Strongly for cutting red tape, with a common-sense approach
economy.summary: Platform pledges to 'support local businesses to thrive' and to 'ensure big business and industry fairly and transparently contribute to our community.' He points to the forestry era as a lesson that industry revenue must leave lasting community assets.
economy.quote: We need to ensure that the benefits industry brings continue to serve Squamish long after that industry leaves.

parking.position: Build a parkade; paid parking for visitors, free for locals; a moratorium on parking variances
parking.summary: Sean had said little in public about this before answering our questionnaire. Sean’s own answers are below.

compass.rationale: Leans modestly left economically: a career building non-market housing, asking for public land to be reserved for non-profit housing, new public recreation amenities and making industry pay more; offset by a 2027 property tax freeze and sharp criticism of District spending and overruns. Socially he leads a youth-homelessness supportive housing non-profit and wants environmental monitoring of industry, but has made no statements on policing or enforcement, so the social value is kept modest.

answer_notes.q1: We've grown faster than our infrastructure and amenities can keep up with, so we need to slow down, catch up, and stop approving development just to hit provincial housing numbers.
answer_notes.q2: Height isn't the question for me — it's whether a project actually delivers what residents need.
answer_notes.q3: In general, I support developing within our growth boundary where we can. But every new project should be judged on its own merits and whether it delivers affordability and increased quality of life for all residents
answer_notes.q4: I'll increase the amount of affordable housing developers need to provide, bring resident-restricted affordable home ownership to Squamish, and leverage federal funding effectively to deliver affordable housing.
answer_notes.q5: The slated Pioneer Way and Hearth and Home projects must go ahead to meet the need, but they must be designed in partnership with residents in appropriate locations.
answer_notes.q6: We need sufficient policing to maintain public safety, but we need to pair it with effective preventative approaches and services that address the root causes of people feeling unsafe.
answer_notes.q7: I've pledged to freeze property taxes for 2027 after years of huge increases. Government needs to be forced to use our funds more effectively rather than putting greater pressure on residents.
answer_notes.q23: I called on the current Council to reject this deal so a new Council could negotiate one that actually delivers for Squamish, including a real recreation centre.
answer_notes.q8: Woodfibre is here to stay - we need to use every tool available to ensure we protect our people's health, our air and water quality, and leave a meaningful legacy to Squamish.
answer_notes.q9: Climate action is a crucial long-term priority: but environmental measures shouldn't make life harder or more expensive for residents in the short-term.
answer_notes.q10: I constantly hear that red tape  slow down residents who want to contribute to our community. I'll take a common-sense approach that enforces expectations without cumbersome bureaucracy.
answer_notes.q11: Regional transit could bring huge benefit to affordability and quality of life, but I'll push provincial and federal governments to contribute their fair share.
answer_notes.q37: I'll place a moratorium on parking variances so developers provide enough parking for the people who'll actually live there.
answer_notes.q12: Brennan Park's real needs — a bigger pool, a second sheet of ice, better change rooms — have to get fixed, and I'll aim to fund it through a fair deal with industry instead of debt that pushes up costs for locals.
answer_notes.q18: This is a complex issue, and any decision should be made in partnership with all the people affected - including service users, social service organizations, and local neighbors - not dictated by Mayor and Council.
answer_notes.q31: Clearing an encampment with nowhere for people to go just moves the problem down the street — the real fix is the housing and services that prevent it in the first place, while enforcement should focus on illegal and antisocial behaviour.
answer_notes.q34: Making Squamish a place where everyone feels safe is important - but residents haven't raised this as a major need currently.
answer_notes.q13: I'll increase the share of affordable units developers are required to deliver - we've seen that simply building more units has not led to housing that is more affordable, so we need to change our approach.
answer_notes.q14: Decisions like this should be made alongside residents affected by specific projects.
answer_notes.q15: Our land and resources should be used for our long-term benefit, not sold off for short-term profit or to pay off government debt.
answer_notes.q16: I haven't heard from residents that this is a major issue, but every home taken off the long-term rental market is one less home for a local family.
answer_notes.q17: Yes - both safe spaces and a permit system for vehicle residents, built together with the people it affects, will give everyone a safe place to sleep and the right to quiet enjoyment.
answer_notes.q19: More enforcement without more support just shifts the problem — I want a downtown that's safe because people's real needs are being met.
answer_notes.q20: Government investment should address the root cause of issues, not just the symptoms. And local services need to collaborate effectively to deliver for all residents needs.
answer_notes.q21: I agree that the public should have a say in major projects, but I plan to build more effective community engagement throughout project development, not wait until the last minute to hold a referendum.
answer_notes.q22: Renewing Brennan Park is a huge priority, but it should be paid for by a fair deal with industry, not more public debt that will increase costs to residents in the long term.
answer_notes.q24: This is a real trade-off between upfront cost and long-term savings that deserves thoughtful consideration for each project, not a blanket rule.
answer_notes.q25: We should introduce paid parking for visitors and tourists, with free parking for locals. And more importantly, we need to invest in a parkade to accommodate growing tourism.
answer_notes.q36: Parking is driving people away from downtown, and identifying a location for a parkade is one of the things I want to move on - it can pay for itself in a relatively short timeframe.
answer_notes.q38: Locals shouldn't have to pay more to live here and access basic amenities, including downtown. But we should leverage more revenue from tourists who come to visit our town.
answer_notes.q26: I'd put a moratorium on new active transportation upgrades until there's been real community engagement - residents are saying this is not a big priority for public funds while we have other pressing issues.
answer_notes.q27: Squamish needs both thriving industry and residents who can afford to live here - we should be open-minded about the best use of each piece of land in the long-term.
answer_notes.q28: Flood protection is essential infrastructure, but I'll look at how to fund it without piling more cost onto residents who are already stretched.
answer_notes.q29: The Squamish Nation are our closest neighbors and partners: working more effectively with them will lead to better outcomes for all of us.
answer_notes.q30: Childcare is a huge need, and we should prioritize projects that deliver greater affordability to residents.
answer_notes.q32: These two things should not be pitted against each other: our approach should ensure the safety of all residents - those facing homelessness and their neighbors.
answer_notes.q33: Locations should be chosen based on what makes sense for the project, which should be designed alongside both future and current residents.
answer_notes.q35: Everyone should be held accountable to local laws, and that has to go hand in hand with real services that address why open drug use is happening in the first place.

own_words.one_thing: Making Squamish tangibly more affordable for residents on average incomes.
own_words.say_no: My vote will always align with the greatest needs of residents, and I'll ensure I'm engaging with them to understand how I'll vote: the job of Mayor is to represent them. I'll strive to build consensus among Mayor and Council so we can make the right decisions and move on to action.
own_words.homelessness: Encampments and street disorder come from the same root cause: not nearly enough housing people can afford. My plan is to expedite Pioneer Way's supportive housing, get Hearth and Home built with community input on location, and have RCMP, bylaw, and social services working the same plan instead of separate ones — while holding everyone accountable to the law. I don't have a costed number to give you today, and I won't invent one. Instead, I'll work to leverage all available provincial and federal funding - including already committed funding -  to ensure minimal cost falls on Squamish taxpayers.
own_words.differently: The Brennan Park renovation. The District spent $21 million — $3 million over budget — and it didn't address what residents actually told them they needed: a bigger pool, a second sheet of ice, better change rooms. I'd have included a new recreation centre in any proposed deal with Woodfibre, then tied spending directly to those stated priorities before a shovel went in the ground. I also would have engaged residents in the design process from the beginning,  to ensure that we sought and leveraged funding to deliver what they actually need.
own_words.disagree: In my experience talking with residents, most of want the same thing: a town that's affordable, with the amenities we need, where everyone feels safe. The disagreement is usually about how to get there, and that's a conversation worth having properly - I'd want to understand what needs they have that are driving their perspective, and how I can take their needs into consideration.
own_words.pitch: Building a Squamish that's affordable, accessible, and accountable - now and for generations to come.

name: Jenna Stoner
occupation_background: Two-term councillor (elected 2018, re-elected 2022). Outside council she has about 15 years' experience in sustainable fisheries and aquaculture at the intersection of business, government and environmental conservation (in 2022 she worked for Sustainable Fisheries Partnership); holds a Master of Marine Management (Dalhousie) and a BSc (UVic). Sees an opportunity to reorient developer amenity contributions (recently focused on childcare and affordable housing) toward Brennan Park and cultural facilities
Supportive and bridge housing: backed the 65-unit Government Road supportive housing lease and pushed for public answers on the BC Housing HEARTH proposal
Would consider a mayor's task force on the unhoused and street disorder (Downtown BIA, RCMP, bylaw, Under One Roof residents and others)
A 'human-centred' approach to vehicle residents, exploring permit programs and safe lots on District-owned parking lots

A community advisory assembly (citizens' assembly model, as in New Westminster), especially for the upcoming OCP renewal; detailed decision explainers, monthly office hours and quarterly in-person events

Keeping growth inside the OCP growth management boundary, with higher-density infill along transit (answers she gave to the 2022 My Sea to Sky candidate survey, run by an environmental advocacy group opposed to Woodfibre LNG; not restated in her 2026 mayoral campaign)
Putting Woodfibre LNG revenue toward capital investment and building asset-management reserves
Bringing BC Housing's HEARTH temporary 'bridge housing' to Squamish, with more public engagement on the site

opposes.text: The Woodfibre LNG project as a whole, which she says runs against climate commitments (while calling herself a pragmatist since it is outside District jurisdiction)

The first Woodfibre LNG floatel permit as applied for in April 2024: one of four councillors who voted it down 4-3, saying there was not enough information. (In July 2025 she voted with the 5-2 majority to approve a two-year permit for two floatels, after adding a shore-power condition.)
The BC Environmental Assessment Office overriding District jurisdiction on the floatel instead of holding the company accountable
The FortisBC pipeline and the Garibaldi at Squamish resort proposal (2022 candidate survey)
Expanding beyond the growth management boundary before the District has met its OCP preconditions (2022, regarding the Cheema lands; she recorded herself as 'neutral' on the proposal itself)
Voted against reopening the camping bylaw's ban on sleeping in vehicles (Apr 2, 2024), saying the bylaw was brought in to address problem behaviour

growth.summary: Accepts that growth will continue and wants to shape it: 'We can't stop that change' (Squamish Reporter, Sept 3, 2026). In 2022 she said she supports the OCP growth management boundary to focus growth within the existing footprint as compact, walkable communities, and pledged support for higher-density infill along transit. Caveat: no specific statement on building heights above six storeys was found, and the boundary statements date from 2022.
growth.quote: I am supportive of the growth management boundary established in the OCP. This helps us focus future growth within our existing footprint.

housing_affordability.position: Pro non-market housing through partnerships; has balanced it against infrastructure funding
housing_affordability.summary: Campaigns on 446 below-market homes built during her eight years (300+ more coming) and sits on the Housing Squamish board. She says pre-zoning alone won't deliver housing for extreme core need or homelessness and that 'other partnership and other models' are needed. She also defended selling District land on Pioneer Way to fund core infrastructure rather than reserving it all for affordable housing, and says amenity contributions could now shift toward recreation and culture.
housing_affordability.quote: There are limited opportunities with public land … to actually advance the issue of affordable housing. We also as a municipality need to provide fire halls and public works facilities.

homelessness.position: Supports supportive and bridge housing; multi-agency task force; human-centred approach
homelessness.summary: Supported the 60-year lease for 65 supportive housing units on Government Road and described BC Housing's proposed temporary HEARTH units as needed bridge housing, while moving a motion to bring BC Housing to a public meeting to answer location concerns. As mayor she would consider a mayor's task force on the unhoused and street disorder and explore safe lots/permits for vehicle residents.
homelessness.quote: I don't think there's ever a welcome place often, unfortunately, to house those who are the most vulnerable in our community. But there are, as for our last Point-In-Time count, 125 individuals who need a home—not in six months, not in 12 months, not in two years, but today.

policing.position: No public position found on RCMP funding; favours multi-agency responses
policing.summary: No statement on RCMP budgets or officer numbers was found. She proposes including the RCMP and bylaw officers in a multi-agency mayor's task force on street disorder, and says a safe-lot program for vehicle residents would not mean bylaw requirements 'just disappear.'
policing.quote: I think it would be unfair to suggest that just because we put in a safe-lots program then all the bylaw requirements just disappear.

taxes_spending.position: Infrastructure-first investment; zero-based budgeting; no tax freeze pledged
taxes_spending.summary: Supported the District's first 10-year financial plan (adopted unanimously; it projected tax increases of about 13% in 2027 and 12.9% in 2028) and adding WLNG tax revenue to asset-management reserves. She defends spending on fire halls, the public works facility and wastewater plant, and now promises zero-based budgeting while making room for amenities like Brennan Park.
taxes_spending.quote: Instead of rolling over budgets year-to-year, taking the time and providing transparency and ensuring every dollar gets accounted for from zero.

environment_lng.position: Opposes WLNG in principle; pragmatic about securing benefits; climate action a priority
environment_lng.summary: Says she does not support the Woodfibre LNG project because fossil fuel expansion conflicts with climate commitments, but as a 'pragmatist' focuses on securing benefits for Squamish. She was one of four councillors who voted down the first floatel permit in April 2024, saying there was not enough information, and publicly criticized the province's override; in July 2025 she voted with the 5-2 majority to approve a two-year permit for two floatels after adding a shore-power condition. She also voted in favour of FortisBC's workers' lodge temporary use permit in 2024, which council rejected 4-3. She cites getting a climate emergency resolution passed unanimously in her first term (source: 2022 re-election release), made 15 of 16 climate commitments in the 2022 candidate survey run by My Sea to Sky, an advocacy group opposed to Woodfibre LNG, and lists the climate crisis among her advocacy priorities. Her vote on the proposed 10-year WLNG agreement (scheduled Sept 22, 2026) was not yet known at time of research.
environment_lng.quote: I don't support the project as a whole. I think the continued development of fossil fuels goes against our local, provincial and federal commitments, and international commitments on climate. I'm also a pragmatist and a realist.

transportation.position: Advocate for regional transit and transit expansion; supports active transportation
transportation.summary: Lists transit expansion among issues she would press the province on and cites regional transit advocacy through her SLRD role. In a 2022 survey she committed to advocating for regional transit, investing in local transit and investing in active transportation networks. Parking was one of her most frequent motion topics on council, but no current campaign position on paid parking or a parkade was found.
transportation.quote: Sitting at the SLRD table has allowed me to work with partners across the region on big issues that we know Squamish can't solve alone such as solid waste management, advocacy on regional transit, and regional growth management strategies.

economy.position: Support small business and community organizations; economic diversification
economy.summary: Her priorities page talks about 'supporting the people, small businesses, and community organizations that make Squamish awesome,' and in March 2026 she listed economic growth and diversification among the top issues facing Squamish. No detailed campaign proposals on employment lands, tourism or downtown were found.

parking.position: Usually lets the market decide how much parking a building needs; voted to make paid parking a priority; no 2026 campaign statement
parking.summary: No parking position in her 2026 campaign material. On council she moved the 2023 motion that started the paid-parking plan, seconded and voted for the defeated April 2024 motion to make paid parking by the end of 2025 a council priority, moved the 2025 bylaw removing parking minimums for six-unit lots near future frequent transit, and moved a 2025 motion to improve accessible parking downtown sooner than 2027. She called herself 'a very avid proponent of letting the market determine how much parking is necessary' while saying a 40% cut at University Highlands went too far. In 2022 she said the District should understand the problem before spending 'on new systems or infrastructure'.
parking.quote: I am usually a very avid proponent of letting the market determine how much parking is necessary and I am the first to be a little bit sad about the fact that we might be turning down 32 affordable units, but this feels like it's too far of a parking reduction for the location that we’re talking about.

compass.rationale: Eight-year record of supporting infrastructure-driven budgets with large tax increases, non-market housing via Housing Squamish, climate-emergency policy and supportive housing, plus opposition in principle to Woodfibre LNG, place her left of centre on both axes. This is tempered by self-described pragmatism (she voted down the first floatel permit in 2024 but approved a two-year permit in 2025), zero-based budgeting, support for selling public land to fund infrastructure and a low formal dissent rate.

name: Eric Andersen
occupation_background: Grew up in Squamish and returned after years working elsewhere. Employment background in forestry, wood products and transportation, plus research and communications consulting; has worked with the Squamish Historical Society and was described by the Squamish Chief as someone many look to as a keeper of local history. Two-term councillor (2018-2026).
tagline: “A vote for Eric Andersen for Squamish Council is a vote for good jobs close to home.” (slogan from his previous campaigns)
top_priorities: Avoiding unbalanced growth - jobs, businesses and amenities keeping pace with population
Good jobs close to home / a complete community (Smart Growth) — 2014 and 2022 platforms
Employment-lands and sector strategies for forestry, wood products, the port and tourism — 2022 platform
Relationships with Squamish Nation, the province and the federal government
Planning for recreation and cultural facilities

supports.text: Balanced growth: jobs, businesses and amenities keeping pace with population growth
Land strategies for key job sectors - forestry, wood products manufacturing, port lands, tourism-commercial land (2022 platform; no 2026 statement found)
Approving the Woodfibre LNG floatel permit (voted against denial in 2024; voted for the two-floatel permit in 2025) and building a working relationship with WLNG
Voted in favour of a temporary use permit for FortisBC's workers' lodge (defeated 3-4, 2024)
Garibaldi Estates pre-zoning readings (supported, while saying they are not the whole answer to housing)
Delegating more development-permit decisions to staff to streamline review (voted in support, Feb 2026)
Stronger advocacy to senior governments on attainable housing; negotiating affordable units with the Housing Society involved (2022 platform)
Updated long-term facility roadmaps so Squamish is ready when outside funding appears
Integrating supportive housing into residential neighbourhoods — calls existing Squamish examples 'success stories'

opposes.text: Allowing six units (with no off-street parking minimum) within 400 m of a future frequent bus route - voted against; 'I'm uncomfortable with how far it goes'
Neighbourhood commercial node zoning on The Boulevard in Garibaldi Highlands - sole vote against (Jan 2026), wanted fuller report on community feedback
Revised (scaled-back) 1032 Finch Drive townhouse rezoning with an added sunset clause - sole vote against, Dec 2025; his reasons were not reported
Joining the Sue Big Oil class action (voted against at Oct 2023 committee of the whole; called it a 'complex picture')
Growth where Squamish mostly sells 'the right to live here' and over-relies on residential taxes (2022 campaign announcement)

growth.summary: In the 2022 election he answered a questionnaire from My Sea to Sky, an anti-LNG advocacy group, in his own words: he said he was supportive of the Cheema Lands and North Crumpit proposals, giving as his reason that Squamish has 'too many competing uses of scarce valley bottom lands' and 'must learn to build housing on upper slopes responsibly', and opposed to Garibaldi at Squamish because 'scale of proposed development is a big concern'. These are 2022 answers.
growth.quote: I am in alignment with Councillor Greenlaw's concerns, in particular with the 400 metre distance. I'm uncomfortable with how far it goes.

housing_affordability.position: Negotiate affordable units, cut developer process costs, lobby senior governments
housing_affordability.summary: In 2022 he called for continued negotiation of affordable units with the Housing Society involved, lower processing and transaction costs for developers, construction innovation (including wood products) and much more advocacy to senior governments. No 2026 campaign statement on housing found.
housing_affordability.quote: I think we shouldn't limit ourselves to the powers that we have. I mean, as a municipality, I think we need to be doing more strategic advocacy, vis-à-vis the federal and provincial [...] governments. (2022)

homelessness.position: Voted for Government Road supportive housing lease; stresses neighbour relations and design
homelessness.summary: Part of the unanimous July 2026 vote endorsing a 60-year lease for 65 supportive homes at 39900 Government Road. He raised nearby residents' concerns, said relationship-building with neighbours is central, and asked for aesthetics similar to Spirit Creek. No broader public statement on encampments found.

taxes_spending.position: Grow the industrial/business tax base to relieve residential taxpayers; plan facilities before funding them
taxes_spending.summary: Voted with the rest of council to adopt the 2026-2035 financial plan (12.8% tax revenue increase for 2026). His long-standing argument is that Squamish over-relies on residential taxes and needs a bigger employment and industrial tax base. On facilities he stresses having updated plans ready for outside funding.
taxes_spending.quote: We understand there's impatience in the community with respect to facilities. But unless we have updated roadmaps and adequate plans, we won't be ready when funding sources come along.

environment_lng.position: Pro-permit on Woodfibre LNG; climate action via local jobs, wood construction and adaptation
environment_lng.summary: ... In 2022 he framed forestry and wood products as 'green tech' and climate action. In the same 2022 My Sea to Sky survey that records his support for Cheema Lands and North Crumpit, he also committed to 14 of the group's 16 climate actions - including advocating that the province let local governments ban new gas hookups, protecting natural assets, a biodiversity conservation strategy and adopting the doughnut-economics model - declining only the fossil fuel non-proliferation treaty and Sue Big Oil.
environment_lng.quote: I support natural gas as a 'bridging fuel', and I support WLNG's ongoing efforts to protect (and enhance, through extensive site remediation investments) the local marine environment. (2022)

transportation.position: Reduce commuting through local jobs; supports regional transit options; realistic about parking demand
transportation.summary: In 2022 he backed regional transit options (including fast-ferry technology), said Squamish has diverse parking problems needing new facilities and enforcement, and proposed wood-built parkades designed for re-purposing. In 2025 he voted against removing parking minimums for six-unit lots near future frequent transit. No 2026 statement found.

economy.position: Jobs-first: protect employment lands and build sector strategies
economy.summary: His signature issue. Wants land-use strategies for forestry, wood manufacturing, port lands, tourism and logistics, and warns that re-zoning former industrial land has left Squamish unprepared for high-wage employers.
economy.quote: What we are selling to the rest of the world from Squamish is mostly the right to live here. This is unbalanced and unsustainable. We can do better. (2022 campaign announcement)

parking.position: Council's most consistent voice for more parking: wants developer cash-in-lieu spent on off-street parking facilities and has voted against removing parking minimums
parking.summary: In April 2026 he voted against sending $210,000 of developer cash-in-lieu to the alternative-transportation fund, saying it should go to the Off-Street Parking Facilities Reserve Fund. He voted against the 2025 bylaw removing parking minimums for six-unit lots near future frequent transit, and told council he did not support cutting parking at University Highlands. In 2022 he said Squamish has 'diverse parking problems' needing 'new facilities and regulations/ enforcement', and proposed wood-built parkades designed so they can be re-purposed. He voted for the paid-parking pilot but against making paid parking a 2025 priority and against studying community-wide paid parking. No 2026 campaign statement found.
parking.quote: We are overlooking, in our planning for the downtown, the need for off-street parking facilities and here is an example of where we can take advantage of an opportunity to put some dollars into that fund.

compass.rationale: Consistently pro-industry (forestry, port, Woodfibre LNG and FortisBC permits), wants lower developer processing costs and a bigger industrial tax base, and voted against joining Sue Big Oil - but he also favours active municipal land-use strategies and supported council budgets and non-market housing projects. Little evidence on social or policing questions, so the social score stays near centre.

name: John French
occupation_background: Born and raised in Squamish; his parents and sister live in town and his children were raised there. Two-term councillor (2018-2026). Occupation outside council not stated on his 2026 campaign material reviewed here.
top_priorities: Community First - parks, recreation, trails, library, seniors' space, family events
Housing affordability and more diverse housing forms (tiny homes, ADUs, suites, co-living)
Regional transit from Mount Currie/Whistler to West Vancouver
Environment - growth planned around maximum environmental preservation, infill first
Starting the Official Community Plan update as soon as possible
Team work: show up, listen, put the community first

supports.text: More housing of all kinds, with infill, secondary suites, ADUs, tiny homes and co-living; treating developers 'like partners' while the District keeps the final say
Faster, more cost-effective permitting - long waits for builders add to the price of new housing
The Squamish housing society's work on below-market housing for the local workforce
Regional transit to West Vancouver and Whistler, 15-minute local service downtown-Garibaldi Estates, and pushing the province and Ottawa to fund it
Bike lanes, safer pedestrian infrastructure and better transit - argued as also reducing congestion for those who must drive
Housing plus health care for unhoused people downtown ('a roof over their head and health care')
Woodfibre LNG floatel permit - voted against denial (2024), moved the 2025 two-year approval, and voted against the shore-power condition added to it
Zero-based budgeting discussion, and grants, reserves, community fundraising and private partnerships to pay for Brennan Park
Keeping the proposed HEARTH temporary housing OFF the X̱wún̓eḵw waterfront park site ('fully unacceptable') while pursuing other locations

opposes.text: Property tax increases projected for the next five years, which he says are too high
Campaign over-promising - 'It takes four people to get anything done'
Cautious about expanding outside the growth management boundary - acknowledges the opportunity but says it would be very costly for the municipality
Height variances that heavily shade neighbours - called a Valleycliffe proposal 'simply unsupportable' on shadow impacts
Council infighting and 'petty squabbles'

growth.summary: Pro-supply and comfortable with Squamish's shift to denser housing forms, driven in his words by finance and land scarcity; infill is 'a key goal'. He acknowledges room to expand outside the growth boundary but says it would be very costly. Has backed most development permits but balks at height where shadowing is severe. (In a 2022 advocacy-group survey he was listed as supportive of Cheema Lands, North Crumpit and Garibaldi at Squamish.) No statement specifically about buildings above six storeys was found: he has supported five- and six-storey downtown projects while opposing a large height variance in Valleycliffe on shadowing grounds, so his score on the taller-buildings statement is an inference from that pattern.
growth.quote: Single-family dwellings were the dominant housing form for decades and it's a housing form that has become the housing form of the elite in Squamish.

housing_affordability.position: More supply, faster permits, diverse forms, plus the housing society
housing_affordability.summary: Frames affordability as demand exceeding supply. Wants developers treated as partners, cost-effective permitting with monitored wait times, and more ADUs, suites and tiny homes; supports the housing society creating below-market workforce housing.
housing_affordability.quote: We need more of it, and we need to find ways to provide more housing at pricing that is accessible to young people, seniors and those living with fixed and low incomes.

homelessness.position: Housing and health care first; also wants encampment complaints resolved
homelessness.summary: Calls helping unhoused people downtown with mental-health struggles the biggest challenge of the next four years. Voted for the Government Road supportive-housing lease. In a 2025 blog post he described frustration at the lack of action on the camp behind Under One Roof and personally working to get one camper into housing.
homelessness.quote: The help they need is a roof over their head and health care.

policing.summary: No clear position on RCMP staffing or budgets found. He has done an RCMP ride-along, asked at council whether the Car 99 program patrols encampments, and cited RCMP wages as part of what the 2026 budget pays for.

taxes_spending.position: Voted for the 2026 budget but says projected increases are too high; wants zero-based budgeting
taxes_spending.summary: Supported the 2026-2035 financial plan (12.8% 2026 increase) while warning it would push some residents out of Squamish. For 2026 he says the five-year projected increases are too high and wants the next council to discuss zero-based budgeting; for Brennan Park he points to grants, reserves, community fundraising and private partnerships.
taxes_spending.quote: Zero-based budgeting is something that I want this next council to have a conversation on.

environment_lng.position: Pro-permit on Woodfibre LNG; environment protected through infill and transit
environment_lng.summary: In a 2022 candidate survey run by My Sea to Sky (an advocacy group opposed to the project) he answered that he was 'supportive' of Woodfibre LNG, the FortisBC pipeline, the workcamp and the floatel, writing that 'Canadian energy is ethically produced' and that Canada should 'share its energy wealth.' On council he voted for the WLNG floatel permit in April 2024 (one of three in a 3-4 defeat), saying 'Denying this permit is not going to stop the project that's currently under construction'; moved the July 2025 two-year approval and voted against Coun. Stoner's successful shore-power amendment to it; and voted for the FortisBC workers' lodge permit. Counter-signal: he voted in favour of joining Sue Big Oil at the Oct 24, 2023 committee vote. His platform calls the environment one of Squamish's best assets, protected by smart planning and infill.

transportation.position: Strong regional-transit advocate; active transportation; parking is a management problem
transportation.summary: Wants regular corridor bus service from Mount Currie to West Vancouver and 15-minute local service, funded with provincial and federal help. Supports bike lanes and pedestrian safety, moved the 30 km/h downtown limit, and argues (citing Shoup and Grabar) that downtown has a parking-management problem and needs usage data.
transportation.quote: A transit service from Mount Currie to West Vancouver was needed years ago.

economy.position: Limited 2026 detail; partnership with Squamish Nation and builders
economy.summary: His 2026 platform has no dedicated economy plank. He highlights District-Squamish Nation agreements as enabling future infrastructure (water and sewer, waste, recreation, housing). His site hosts 2022 posts on industrial land and tourism, not reviewed in detail here.

parking.position: Says downtown has a parking management problem, not a supply problem; wants usage data; backed on-street pay parking in 2022
parking.summary: In an Aug. 2026 blog post he concludes, after reading Shoup and Grabar, that 'what we have in Squamish is a parking management problem', lists downtown lots and garages he finds rarely full, and calls for data on how parking in new buildings is actually used. He quotes Grabar's call to abolish parking minimums and charge for the best street parking, without saying he would do the same. In 2022 he wrote 'I support an on-street pay parking program in the commercial area' and said he would not support losing more street stalls to vendors. On council he voted in April 2024 to prioritise traffic calming over paid parking by 2025, voted against studying community-wide paid parking, and voted for the six-unit/no-parking-minimum bylaw. He called a 40% parking cut at University Highlands 'a little bit exciting'.
parking.quote: From these thinkers who have spent a significant amount of time researching and studying parking I concluded what we have in Squamish is a parking management problem.

compass.rationale: Leans market-friendly on housing supply, permitting speed, zero-based budgeting and LNG permits, but also supports public spending on transit, recreation and the non-market housing society and voted for the 12.8% budget. Socially he favours a housing-and-health-care approach to homelessness, active transportation and reconciliation; he has also written of frustration at slow action on the downtown encampment while complaints mounted.

name: Andrew Hamilton
occupation_background: Instructor of Computing and Data Science at Capilano University with a PhD in physics (University of Alberta); worked at CERN on the Higgs boson discovery and has lived in the US, Switzerland and South Africa. Husband and father of two; one-term councillor (2022-2026). Built bcmunicipaldata.org to let residents explore BC property tax data.
tagline: “Squamish is amazing.” Open consultation, respectful debate, transparent decisions.
top_priorities: Fiscally and environmentally sustainable core infrastructure
Fair and responsible development zoning
Reasonable and reliable recreation amenities
Realistic capital-project planning, cost forecasting and delivery

Spending tax money efficiently

supports.text: Infill density over greenfield sprawl as the more economically and environmentally sustainable way to add housing supply

Parking reform: priced on-street parking (e.g. Cleveland Ave) to manage demand, with revenue returned to the affected area such as the Downtown BIA (his campaign site also calls for removing off-street parking minimums)
Better capital-project lifecycle budgeting - realistic cost forecasts, escalation mitigation, efficient execution

Self-funded campaign under $500 with no donations

opposes.text: Free on-street parking and mandatory parking minimums, which he says create shortages and hide costs in food, housing and taxes

Most of the Garibaldi Estates pre-zoning - voted against three of the five bylaw votes on May 19 2026, objecting to pre-zoning for densities staff said were not financially viable and to treating one neighbourhood differently from the rest of town (he supported the two he judged viable: the ground-oriented residential zone and the District-led rezoning of 2163 Mamquam Road)
Permissive property tax exemptions for the Squamish Valley Golf Club and Sea to Sky Montessori (voted against, 2023-2024)
The 2024 Woodfibre LNG floatel permit as drafted - said the $2M security deposit was too low (he also voted against denying it)
Joining the Sue Big Oil class action (voted against at Oct 2023 committee of the whole; reasons not stated)
Council making advocacy its main focus - he calls advocacy 'a necessary role' but says council shouldn't spend all its time on it at the expense of what is within its jurisdiction

growth.summary: States a general preference for infill density over greenfield sprawl and wants zoning that lets supply keep pace with demand. In practice he is a stickler for the zoned rules rather than a height opponent: he voted for the six-to-seven-storey Three Summits downtown development (Jan 2024) and seconded the six-unit transit-oriented zoning bylaw (Sept 2025), but voted against the seven-storey 38026 Second Avenue permit (June 2025) because it needed a height variance, saying council should stop granting height variances and change the zoning instead; he made the same point about the size, not the principle, of the Valleycliffe height variance. On the Garibaldi Estates pre-zoning (May 2026) he opposed three of the five bylaw votes and supported two, objecting to pre-zoning for densities staff said were not financially viable while stating he agreed with the neighbourhood plan itself.
growth.quote: Generally, I believe infill development (density) will lead to a more economically and environmentally sustainable community compared to greenfield development (sprawl).

housing_affordability.position: Supply through zoning; reduce parking mandates that raise housing costs
housing_affordability.summary: Sees zoning as council's most direct long-term lever and frames affordability as high demand meeting limited land. Argues removing parking minimums would relieve pressure on housing costs. No public statement found on the housing society, DCCs/ACCs or inclusionary zoning.
housing_affordability.quote: Let's reduce the pressure on the housing stock in our community, increase the housing stock in our community, and make it more affordable for folks to live here.

homelessness.position: Voted for supportive housing; asks residents to propose alternative sites rather than only object
homelessness.summary: Part of the unanimous July 2026 vote for the Government Road supportive-housing lease, where he questioned BC Housing on building trust with the community. On the temporary housing site for the downtown encampment he urged residents to suggest alternatives once a site is announced.
homelessness.quote: If you don't think this site should be selected, please take the next step and suggest which sites should.

policing.summary: No public position found on RCMP staffing or budgets. (Emergency services is his second most common authored-motion topic in the voting record, but that reflects procedure rather than a stated stance.)

taxes_spending.position: Accepts increases if money is spent efficiently; strict on project costing and permissive tax exemptions
taxes_spending.summary: Voted for the 2026-2035 plan despite misgivings about absorbing capital cost overruns. Names reforming how property tax rates are calculated as his top accomplishment, has the most property-tax dissents on council (mostly against permissive exemptions), moved a failed 2025 amendment to cut the Brennan Park line item, and warns projects such as the Pemberton-Laurelwood bridge are under-costed.
taxes_spending.quote: It's very easy to say somebody else should pay, but if somebody else is paying, they're part of our community, and we are paying.

environment_lng.position: Swing vote on Woodfibre LNG; climate action through enabling individual choices
environment_lng.summary: The only member to vote against both denying and approving the floatel in April 2024 (he wanted a security deposit nearer $10M), then voted to reconsider and voted for the two-floatel permit in 2025; voted against the FortisBC lodge permit and against joining Sue Big Oil. Says climate change is human-caused and council's role is infrastructure that lets people choose lower-carbon options. On WLNG money, says the town has many capital needs to prioritise.
environment_lng.quote: There is no question in my mind that the Earth's climate is changing due to the carbon that humans are emitting into our atmosphere.

transportation.position: Market-based parking reform; supports cycling and transit; voted against the 30 km/h downtown zone
transportation.summary: His most detailed issue: pay parking where demand is highest ('not a revenue thing'), revenue kept local, and no parking minimums. Usually rides an e-bike when working in town and supports bike infrastructure and more frequent transit. Voted against the Dec 2024 motion that set the 30 km/h downtown limit and asked staff to scope a 40 km/h limit elsewhere; his reasons were not found in the sources reviewed. No statement found on regional transit funding.
transportation.quote: It's not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system.

economy.summary: No specific economic-development platform found beyond wanting people to be able to work in town and returning parking revenue to the Downtown BIA.

parking.position: Price street parking, keep the revenue local, and remove parking minimums
parking.summary: Parking is his most developed issue. His campaign site endorses Donald Shoup's three reforms: charge the right price for on-street parking, spend the revenue on the metered streets, and 'Remove off-street parking requirements.' He told the Chief pay parking on Cleveland Avenue is 'not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system', with revenue possibly going to the Downtown BIA. On council he said his preference was paid parking 'everywhere, all at once', moved the defeated motions to make paid parking a 2025 priority and to study it community-wide, moved the amendment deleting the resident pass from the Darrell Bay pilot, seconded the six-unit/no-parking-minimum bylaw and removed the parking minimum for Garibaldi Highlands cafes. His site's 'ice cream' analogy argues a municipal parking lot ends up subsidised by property tax. A Squamish Reporter opinion piece says he supported a downtown parkade in 2022; I could not find the original 2022 statement.
parking.quote: It's not a revenue thing. It's a management of the system.

compass.rationale: Reasons explicitly from market economics (cites Sowell and Shoup; price parking, drop parking mandates, oppose tax exemptions, spending efficiency, realistic project costing) yet accepted double-digit tax increases as necessary. Accepts climate science and favours cycling/transit and supportive housing, but voted against Sue Big Oil and the 30 km/h zone and says advocacy, while necessary, should not crowd out work within council's own jurisdiction.

name: Chris Pettingill

Former board member of Squamish Arts, Tourism Squamish, the Chamber of Commerce (chair) and Inside Edge (chair), co-founder of Amped in the Park, and a former chair of the BC Green Party.
tagline: “Focus on what matters.” Independent; accepts no campaign donations.
top_priorities: Housing & Affordability
Livability
Safety & Security (emergency readiness, flood and wildfire protection)
Reconciliation, Equity and Climate Action guiding every decision

Waiving DCCs and fees for affordable housing developments; below-market rents tied to both income and market rates

growth.position: Grow inside the boundary — density downtown and near transit, no sprawl
growth.summary: Wants Squamish to meet provincial housing targets by adding density inside the existing growth boundary rather than expanding onto new land: “We can’t put a barricade on the highway.” He is council’s second most frequent dissenter on development items, but those votes are mostly about parking, employment space and amenities rather than height — on the seven-storey 38026 Second Avenue permit he said he was fine with the height and voted no over the cut to required employment space.
growth.quote: In general, I would be okay with the height and even parking reduction, but I'm not okay with the employment reduction even at 20%, given the zoning.

housing_affordability.position: Strong supporter of non-market housing; leans toward deeper subsidies
housing_affordability.summary: Backs the Squamish Housing Society as workforce 'middle housing', waived DCCs/fees for affordable projects, and amenity policies that extract more affordable units and childcare. Says that as the province falls short, council may need to consider deeper subsidies, and that he personally leans that way while wanting community input on the trade-off.
housing_affordability.quote: I think we may need to consider deeper levels of housing subsidy. The trade-off is that deeper subsidies take more taxpayer resources... Personally, I would lean in this direction.

homelessness.position: Supportive housing and provincial programs; opposes a permit system for vehicle dwellers and says a municipal safe lot is not a priority
homelessness.summary: Lists the Government Road supportive housing approval and HEART & HEARTH acceptance among his accomplishments and lobbies the province on homelessness, addictions and mental health through the LMLGA. For people living in vehicles he prioritises affordable and supportive housing, opposes a permit system, says a municipal safe lot is not a priority, and suggests church parking lots could help.

policing.position: Sceptical of using police for mental-health and social needs (2020); no recent statement found
policing.summary: In 2020 he was the lone vote against receiving the RCMP budget report, arguing the province's retreat had forced municipalities to handle mental health and social services through policing, which he called often ineffective. No 2022-2026 statement on RCMP staffing found; his 'Safety & Security' plank is about emergency readiness, flood protection and traffic calming.
policing.quote: We've been forced to essentially deal with mental health and social services using a police force, which is, I think, in many circumstances, an ineffective way of doing that.

taxes_spending.position: Accepts higher taxes to fix the infrastructure deficit
taxes_spending.summary: Voted for the 2026-2035 plan and said earlier years of below-average increases made the 12.8% jump sharper - steadier 8-9% increases might have been better. Campaigns on the $37.8M public works facility, $19.5M+ diking and $21M wastewater upgrades. Open to a recreation-centre P3 but says willing partners are hard to find.
taxes_spending.quote: We may have been better to be at 9% or 8% [increases] year-after-year for several years instead of 4%, 5% and 12%, which is where we find ourselves.

environment_lng.position: Council's most consistent Woodfibre LNG and fossil-gas critic; climate action central
environment_lng.summary: Seconded the 2024 motion to deny the floatel, voted against approval in 2024 and 2025 (seeking a dam assessment and a shorter permit), voted against the FortisBC lodge and for Sue Big Oil. He says his climate objections are separate from the proposed WLNG tax agreement, which should be judged on fairness to other taxpayers. Platform stresses FireSmart, diking and flood management.
environment_lng.quote: Taxation isn't a tool at the municipal level to deal with the climate impacts of a business.

transportation.position: Transit, active transportation and traffic calming; fewer parking mandates
transportation.summary: Supports investing in transit and keeping fares low, lobbies the province for regional transit, and as SLRD director pushes decisions that avoid more Highway 99 congestion. Favours reduced parking requirements and, in 2022, flexible paid parking with revenue spent on downtown and transit; parking is one of his most frequent dissent topics.

economy.position: Match housing growth to employment growth; favours new and core sectors over fossil fuels
economy.summary: Platform calls for 'matching housing development to employment development'. In 2022 he supported focusing on 'new and core economic sectors' more aligned with community values than LNG. Former chair of the Chamber of Commerce and Inside Edge and ex-Tourism Squamish director. No detailed 2026 economic plank found.

parking.position: 'Pretty aggressive on parking reductions'; supports flexible paid parking with revenue spent on downtown and transit
parking.summary: Told the Chief in Sept 2026 that letting developers build less parking eases growing pains, lowers building costs, and that buyers must decide whether a home has enough parking before purchasing. At council he described himself as 'pretty aggressive on parking reductions generally' and 'a proponent of not putting huge investments into parking'. In 2022 he listed 'flexible paid parking to manage demand; spend revenue on improving downtown areas/transit', residential permits, more enforcement and opening empty private stalls to the public. In Dec 2024 he warned against setting an expectation that residents 'should be able to park anywhere for free as long as they want, and it's just tourists that should pay', and he seconded deleting the resident pass from the Darrell Bay pilot. He voted against ratifying that pilot in April 2025; his reason was not found.
parking.quote: It doesn’t seem like a workable variance at this point, even for someone like me who is pretty aggressive on parking reductions generally.

compass.rationale: Favours deeper public housing subsidies, accepts larger tax increases for infrastructure, opposes loosening development oversight and distrusts corporate money in politics. Centres climate action, equity and reconciliation, opposed LNG permits, backs supportive housing and has criticised policing as a response to mental-health needs; he is also a former BC Green Party chair.

name: Janice DesJardins
incumbent_role: Not an incumbent (no record of prior council runs found)

Seniors and long-term-care advocate: Vice Chair of the Vancouver Coastal Association of Family Councils, Co-Chair of the VCH Regional Resident & Family Councils, member of the Independent Long Term Care Councils Association of BC and the Seniors Aging at Home Community Network.
